You are an independent reviewer of an agent-based economic simulation (the Compassionism Simulation) and its findings page, before its next
release. The release makes a corrected price rule the default and regenerates the main figures. The author wants every gap and limitation that
can be addressed fixed before that release. Below: the release step, the current findings-page text, the limits sections of the two latest
studies, and the team's own inventory of open gaps. Answer, numbered:
1. Rank the inventory's items by how much each could change a headline claim or mislead a reader. For each of your top ten, say whether to fix it in the model, fix it in the text, or state it as a limit, and how to verify the fix.
2. Gaps NOT in the inventory that you see in the findings text or the limits (claims without a stated basis, figures resting on design parameters presented as results, missing unfavourable results, comparisons that are not like for like).
3. What the release step itself is missing (checks before publishing, which studies must be rerun on the release engine, what the text must say).
4. Which items are acceptable as stated limits for this release, and why.
Be concrete and short. Do not praise. Plain text.

=== The release step (PLAN.md) ===
### S93 · Release with the private price at the sale as the default
From S92 (decision rule 3 of `prereg/2026-11-s90-private-price-at-sale.md`). Waits on D34 (the version; the author's call). 1. `sp.vAt: 'sale'` becomes the default at that version (`set_version.py`; guard test now differs by design: record it in `dev/DECISIONS.md`). 2. Regenerate the main rows' findings-page data (`data/studies/r2-effects.json` and the cards) from `s90-sale-*-b8ccd8d`, and replace the dated notes with the figures. 3. A Hub corrections-log entry; root-site indexes in step. 4. The late-price figures stay as the v5.9 record (OSF). 5. Then a preregistered amendment deciding which reached studies are rerun on the release engine (readings, financed rows, central bank, history, supply).


=== The findings-page text (dev/reports/s64-findings-page-text.md) ===
# The v5.9 model on the findings page: the text for the v5.9 release

Nov 15, 2026. The words the v5.9 release puts on the findings page for v5.9, beside v5.6. Every sentence comes from the v5.9 reports (`dev/reports/s64-round2-overview.md` and the seven question reports) and follows the preregistered rules of research-update `prereg/2026-11-s63-round2-freeze.md`: the range across the preregistered readings comes before the main row's figure (rule 1); every wealth figure names the price rule it rests on and has its erosion share beside it (rule 6); every inflation figure has the backing statement beside it (rule 4); the financed rows are never led with. Figures are Reference at 20 years unless a sentence says otherwise; the tables give every environment and horizon. Charts: `dev/runs/s64-round2/charts/` (made by `python3 dev/tools/s64_charts.py`; `index.html` previews them with their captions).

The v5.9 release may shorten any paragraph; it may not drop a qualifier that a rule attaches to a figure, or any of the unfavourable results.

## The answer in ten seconds (v5.9)

**Headline cards.** With Compassionism (the full-coverage design, built to meet NEEC's criterion C2.2), against no programme, Reference, 20 years, main row:
- *Below 30 days of basic living:* 0.9% of adult-years, against 19.6% (−18.7 points).
- *Below the cost of living (the basket of essentials):* 3.7% of adult-years, against 36.1% (−32.4 points).
- *Too little wealth (under $25,000), yearly average:* 6.0% of adults, against 24.6% (−18.6 points).
- *Median real wealth at year 20:* $432,300, against $223,900 (+$208,400). Rests on full backing (corrected Nov 17, 2026: it said today's price rule, which full backing barely tests); 1.0% of the gain is the erosion of opening balances (in the programme's favour).

Card footnote (required): "Main row: every dollar the programme pays is matched by new output, as the design states (a design parameter, not a model estimate). The model's own mechanism for new output reaches about 1% of that. See *How much new output backs the payout*."

**One-sentence answer.** Across all 62 preregistered readings, both designs lower all three poverty measures and raise median real wealth, in every environment and at both horizons; the full-coverage design does about 1.4 to 7.1 times as much as the opt-in design. These results hold when every dollar paid is matched by new output, which is the design's statement and not something the model shows; with the model's own backing mechanism, prices rise 15 to 53 points a year.

## How sure we are: the range across readings

Chart: `spec-c22-fgt0PY-20.svg` first (basket poverty), then basic living, wealth poverty and median wealth; programme inflation last. Each has the financed rows beside it.

- Across the 62 preregistered readings, the full-coverage design lowers basket poverty by 25.9 to 33.3 points; at the main row, 32.4 points (seed interval 32.2 to 32.5). The opt-in design lowers it by 16.2 to 22.3 points; at the main row, 20.9 (20.8 to 21.1).
- The full-coverage design lowers adult-years below 30 days of basic living by 16.5 to 19.7 points (main row 18.7) and wealth poverty by 15.7 to 19.7 points (main row 18.6); the opt-in design by 10.7 to 13.0 (12.3) and 9.0 to 12.7 (10.9).
- Across the 62 readings, the full-coverage design raises median real wealth by $187,600 to $659,600; at the main row, $208,400 ($207,100 to $209,900); the opt-in design by $84,600 to $282,100 (main row $99,400). These figures rest on full backing (corrected Nov 17, 2026: this sentence also said they rest on today's price rule, but at full backing almost no unmatched money reaches prices, so the price rule is barely tested there; below full backing they rest on it). Less than 3% of any wealth figure is the erosion of the balances adults held at the start, and it works in the programme's favour: slightly higher prices lower what net debtors owe in real terms (if all wealth were cash, it would work against it, by at most 5.3%). The widest part of the range comes from how much of their spare cash adults spend.
- Every one of these curves is robust: at every reading the effect keeps its sign and its interval excludes zero (48 of 48 poverty and wealth curves, three environments, two horizons). In Stress the opt-in design keeps every sign but loses about two thirds of each effect (basket poverty −7.7 points), because Stress lowers take-up to 40% and the PTF share; the full-coverage design's effects grow there (basket poverty −40.1).

Caption for every curve chart: "Each dot is one preregistered reading, sorted by its effect, with its 95% seed interval. The seed interval covers the model's randomness only, not the choice of reading; the spread of the dots shows that."

## Prices, and how much new output backs the payout

Chart: `backing-c22-20.svg` (and the opt-in design's beside it).

At the main row, programme inflation is 0.0 to 0.2 points a year above no programme, which is no material change, at every reading. **The main row assumes that every dollar the programme pays is matched by new output**, as the design states (a design parameter). The model's own mechanism for new output reaches 0.2 to 1.9% of the payout (14 to 20% if its ceiling is removed). Inflation stays under 5% a year only above about 86 to 90% backing (74 to 77% for the opt-in design in Stress), and runs at 15 to 53 points a year at the mechanism's own point. The poverty effects barely depend on backing; inflation and median wealth do. *Note (Nov 17, 2026):* below full backing, the poverty effects hold because the model has no limit on what the economy can supply. Demand never runs into what can be produced, wages follow prices in full, and the Basic Unit and the cost-of-living basket follow the same prices. With no new output, the real goods the programme's recipients gain are paid for only by holders of savings and lenders, through higher prices. So these figures are not evidence that the design works without backing. At no backing and 40 years, the opt-in design lowers median real wealth.

## Paid for by a contribution instead (shown, never led with)

Chart: the lower row of each curve chart.

If the programme is paid for by a contribution, with the rest borrowed, the full-coverage design needs a mean contribution of 63 to 77% of all money income and lowers basket poverty by at most 17.5 points (in Stress at 20 years it raises it, +0.6); the opt-in design, at 46 to 71% of wages, raises basket poverty by up to 9.6 points. Government debt stays under GDP at the main financed rows, but 46 of the 48 financed poverty and wealth curves are fragile (the two that hold are the opt-in design's basic-living effect in Reference, at both horizons), depending on how the contribution is set up. These rows were run without the weighted top tail.

## Who gains

The full-coverage design lowers the top 1%'s share of wealth by 4.6 points (31.6% to 27.0%) and raises the bottom half's from 2.9% to 9.2%; the opt-in design moves both about half as far. Families in debt fall from 21.9% to 0.7% (full coverage) and 7.4% (opt-in design). In dollars the gains are spread across the distribution, so they are largest in proportion at the bottom: the full-coverage design raises real wealth by $128,000 at the 10th percentile (from −$2,300) and $218,800 at the 90th. Below the top fifth of starting wealth, the slightly higher prices of the programme run lower what adults owe, a gain of 0.5 to 1.7% of their wealth gain; at the top, where money is lent, they are a loss. Adults outside the labour force (disability, early retirement, care, school) stay far more often below the cost of living than adults in it: under the full-coverage design, 8.5 to 16.6% of their adult-years, against 1.8%; under the opt-in design, 28.8 to 58.5%, against 9.5% (no programme: 54 to 82%, against 29%).

## Unfavourable results

Shown together, with the same prominence as the headline:
- Programme inflation is above no programme in every cell: immaterial at the main row, 18 to 53 points a year at no backing.
- Fewer adults work: participation falls 1 to 5 points (adults who leave work for the programme), with their earnings forgone.
- Less movement out of the lowest wealth fifth: 69.8% of adults who start there are still there at year 20 under the full-coverage design, against 66.3% without the programme.
- Labour's share of money income falls by 11.7 to 30.5 points in Reference at 20 years (1.1 to 32.1 across every cell), because the programme's payments are income that is not wages.
- The opt-in design's effects shrink by two thirds in Stress.
- 46 of 48 financed poverty and wealth curves are fragile (the opt-in design's basic-living effect in Reference holds), and the opt-in design paid by a contribution on wages raises basket poverty.

## What no figure here covers

The seed intervals measure the model's randomness only. They do not cover the choice of main row or full backing (a design statement); the readings the screen held fixed; Stress, which was not screened; or the engine's structure: a fixed population in the main row (no ageing, births or deaths; added Nov 17, 2026), one price rule for the whole economy, no central bank, no migration, no value of care, community work or new ventures, PTFs modelled from the Hub's statements and measured costs, 500 adults (a 10,000-adult pair agrees on hours and the top of the wealth distribution). The financed rows leave out the weighted top tail. The model has not been reviewed by an independent economist.

## Where each figure comes from (basis class: simulation release and command)

Engine `104691f` (the frozen model, first published as v5.8), batch shown as v5.9, seeds 1-500, run on GitHub Actions Nov 14-15, 2026, as frozen in research-update `prereg/2026-11-s63-round2-freeze.md` (registered on OSF, https://osf.io/msdzk/overview). Results: compassionism-sim-results `r2-<part>-<env>-<years>-104691f/`; tables `r2-tables-104691f/`; erosion trace `r2-erosion-104691f/`. Commands: `dev/tools/s64_tables.py`, `dev/tools/s64_erosion.js` and `s64_erosion_table.py`, `dev/tools/s64_charts.py`.

=== The automation study: what it means, and its limits (dev/reports/s85-output-per-hour.md, section 13) ===
## 13. What this means, and its limits

**On the author's question.** His view, stated before the run, is that implemented and maintained well the programme can prevent much of the distress automation would cause. The run's answer, in its preregistered terms: **with every adult taking part and every programme dollar backed**, the programme takes away 80-100% of displacement's rise in basket poverty and nearly all of its rise in adults below 30 days of basic living, in every environment; it takes away 13-40% of the fall in median wealth (13-24% with lost jobs); and the free time displacement brings is mostly secure. **With the opt-in design**, it takes away much less, and with lost jobs it often makes the rise in poverty larger. **And the backing is not produced**: the programme's own work, as measured here, matches at most 18% of the payout, and at that backing prices rise 18-71% a year at 20 years (up to 82% at 40). "Prevents much of the distress" is not one of the preregistered categories, so the run gives the shares above instead.

**Limits, stated in advance:**

- No demand shortfall: owners' lower spending out of the dividend is not modelled (the cautious side for the design, whose spending would fill it).
- Prices follow the engine's quantity rule with no central-bank response (the central-bank study is separate), and the model is not a general-equilibrium model: wages, employment and prices outside the essentials do not adjust to one another. At inflation of 20-80% a year a real central bank, and real wage setting, would respond; the inflation figures measure the size of the unbacked money, not a forecast of prices.
- Lower prices from automation reach buyers only through the pass-through to pay.
- Lost jobs count adults, not hours, because hours are not tied to occupation in the engine. There is one ranking for the run; new occupations enter only through the net displacement.
- The dividend raises no investment, so no capital deepening in either run.
- One pass-through for every wage level; the low-paid may get less.
- Contract pay values a programme hour below many workers' own wage (the cautious side for the backing).
- The model's adults are 25 to 64, so part of the households' equity share belongs to older households outside the model.
- Not modelled: the corporate revenue tax (a separate study), health and security raising output per hour (no opened source sizes it), and the Creative Collectives' lending to start-ups (a later step).
- The produced share depends on m, which the design does not state; every statement here names it.
- The trace splits the adults into those who would take part and those who would not, which are fixed groups of latent adults, not the adults enrolled in a given year; it decomposes a difference and does not test a cause by switching something off.
- The preregistered savings measure was run only for the headline rows (the supplementary run). The sensitivity rows read the batch's nearest stored measure, adult-years below 30 days of basic living, and say so; it is not the preregistered measure and moves differently (with full coverage it offsets 97-102% of displacement's rise, where the preregistered measure offsets 66-94%).

## 14. Text for the findings page

> **Automation.** The model was run with 10% to 70% of today's paid work automated away by year 20, as lost jobs or shorter hours, in both the programme and the no-programme run; 50% and 70% are stress readings, beyond the forecasts. With no programme, basket poverty rises by 2 to 13 points and median wealth falls by $7,000 to $48,000. With every adult taking part and full backing, the programme takes away 80-100% of the rise in poverty, 66-94% of the rise in the share of adults with under three months of savings and 13-40% of the fall in wealth, and keeps most of the freed time above the cost of living (4-10% of it below, against 76-81% with no programme). In the opt-in design it takes away much less, and with lost jobs it often makes the rise in poverty larger (and, in the Stress environment at 50% and 70% lost jobs, the rise in low savings). **Full backing is assumed, not produced:** the programme's own work, as the model can measure it, matches 6-17% of the payout at 20 years (5-18% counting the 40-year runs), and at that backing prices rise 48-69% a year in the full-coverage design across the three environments (Reference: 48-63%). Figures are for 20 years. Every cell, favourable or not, is in the study's tables.

## 15. Where everything is

- **Preregistration:** research-update `prereg/2026-11-s85-output-per-hour.md` (Amendment 1: three choices that favoured the programme without a source, fixed before the build; Amendment 2: the sourced values and the build; Amendment 3: the savings measure's supplementary run, the Holm family, the references and the rebuilt checks, before any table was read).
- **Engine:** v5.9.21, `503fa48`; the option is described in MODEL_SPEC section 17. Sources: `sources/s85_output.md`, `sources/s85_values.py`.
- **Job:** compassionism-sim-results `runner/jobs/s85.js` (the supplement: `--sec`).
- **Results:** `s85-{ref,adv,str}-{20,40}-503fa48`, each with `run.txt` and `SHA256SUMS`; the supplement `s85sec-{ref,adv,str}-{20,40}-503fa48` (runs 161-166, each with `run.txt` and `SHA256SUMS`).
- **The trace:** `s85-trace-503fa48` (`python3 dev/tools/s85_trace.py <results> <out>`; the preregistration's fourth amendment fixes it before its figures were computed).
- **Tables:** `s85-tables2-503fa48` (`python3 dev/tools/s85_tables.py <results> <out>`; it replaces `s85-tables-503fa48`, which was written before the supplement was read and is kept as published): the checks, displacement, the readings, the backing produced, shortfalls and free time, together, each at 20 and 40 years, and `s85-summary.json` with every figure and interval.
- **Decisions:** `dev/DECISIONS.md`, the entry of Nov 20, 2026 on reading this study.

=== The supply study: what it means, and its limits (dev/reports/s82-supply-indexing.md, section 11) ===
## 11. What this means, and its limits

**The dated note "the poverty effects barely depend on backing."** Under every supply reading, the programme's effect on poverty still barely depends on backing, and no break-even share appears: that holds with the restricted reading and with the strict bound, at 20 years and 40. In Reference at 20 years:
- with the sourced limit and the market's rule, basket poverty falls 30.6 points at no backing against 32.4 at full backing;
- with the strict bound, 28.9 against 32.4.

What does make the effects depend on backing is how fully wages and the BU keep up with the inflation an unbacked payout causes. If half of the inflation is never made up in wages, the programme with no backing is worse than no programme on basket poverty, and breaks even only at a backed share of 0.08-0.26 (20 years) or 0.30-0.49 (40 years). If wages are made up within a year, they cost 0.3-1.5 points of basket poverty at no backing. A monthly or quarterly BU adjustment, as the design says, costs 0.7-2.7 on its own. These two were not run together; the joint run uses the yearly delay (section 7). Programme inflation itself stays high below full backing in every reading: 40-49 points a year with no backing, under 5 only above about 0.88-0.90.

**Limits, stated:**
1. The limit cuts quantities only. Its unspent money goes to other goods, and it moves no price, so a shortage does not show in wealth, basic living or inflation (section 4). A reading in which a shortage raises prices further, or is saved, is not built.
2. Only housing, medical care and food can be short (the author's narrowing). Other goods, and copied goods such as software, are never cut.
3. The extra need is spread over the three sectors in the basket's proportions. A cut answers last year's gap.
4. Design parameters, swept and labelled wherever shown:
   - the building speed of medical care and food;
   - the essentials' price response θ;
   - the wage readings (wIdx, wc);
   - the BU's delays (the monthly and quarterly ones follow the design's stated adjustment).
5. The BU's relief to the cost of living runs a damped two-year cycle in every programme row, the main row included. It predates this study and is its own inspection step in research-update's plan. *Nov 18:* the cause is the private businesses' lower BU price, which was paid from last year's premium instead of at the sale as the design has it; a fix is built behind an option and its rerun is preregistered (`dev/reports/s90-private-price-at-sale.md`).
6. The ageing reading was rerun after a defect was fixed (section 9). The batch's ageing figures are superseded, not quoted.
7. The population is fixed in every row but the ageing reading.
8. The design's surge protocol (luxury restrictions, conversion limits) is not modelled: the cautious side. The shortages here may be larger than under the design.
9. Building capacity costs nothing in the model's accounts, so the building-speed sweep is a physical sweep, not a fiscal one. The Creative Collectives' lending and output per hour are the next engine step, which is what can make backing produced rather than assumed.
10. the author's views on supply policy (that the levers should be set by the people, and that the design supplies the basics with providers given a reason to supply them) are his and are kept apart from these results. Nothing here tests them.


=== The team's inventory of open gaps (audits/2026-11-20-release-gaps.md) ===
# Gaps and limitations open before the next release (inventory, Nov 20, 2026)

Written in S94 at the author's request: "address all gaps and limitations that we can prior to S93" (the release with the private price at the sale as the default). This inventory is what the outside readers were given (`audits/2026-11-20-pre-release/`). Their readings, and Claude's triage of them into plan steps, are in `audits/2026-11-20-pre-release-triage.md`.

Each item: what the gap is, where it shows, whether it can change a headline, and its status. "Ledger" means the item comes from the ledger's issues list and was not re-checked this session unless it says so.

## A. What the headline rests on
1. **Full backing is assumed in the main row.** Every programme dollar is matched by new output (a design parameter, the design's statement). The engine's own mechanism for new output reaches about 1% of the payout. The automation study's produced backing is 6-17% at 20 years (3-7% opt-in), with programme inflation of 48-69 points a year in full coverage. The findings page carries the footnote and a section. Open decision on the headline cards' headings and the full-backing condition (default: no change). *Can change how a headline reads: yes.*
2. **No limit on total supply below full backing.** A dated note covers the sentences below full backing. The supply-limit study exists but is not in the main row. *Below full backing only.*
3. **The opt-in design does far less than full coverage,** and with lost jobs it makes the rise in poverty larger in 9 of 12 cells. It is published, but the release text should keep it beside any full-coverage headline.

## B. Engine and model gaps
4. **The Creative Collectives' lending to start-ups** (the author, Nov 17 and 19): preregistered Nov 20 (`prereg/2026-11-s94-collectives-lending.md`); build and run to follow.
5. **The late private price** (the BU's two-year swing): fixed behind an option, and the main rows were rerun. The release makes it the default. Item 5 of the release step, deciding which reached studies are rerun on the release engine (readings, financed rows, central bank, history, supply, the suite folders), is not yet preregistered.
6. **The simulation page still uses the Hub's early figures as targets**: `CFG.TARGET_WEALTH` 82000, `TARGET_GINI`, `TARGET_POVERTY`, `TARGET_STABILITY` and a "Target $82K" label on the interactive page (re-checked Nov 20: four occurrences in `index.html`). Research rule 3. *Visible to readers.*
7. **The written description does not describe the validation presets** it is checked by (MODEL_SPEC and ODD; ledger). The validation presets' "Gini" is of wealth less one year of the cost of living times the annual wage, not a wealth Gini.
8. **MODEL_SPEC gaps and contradictions** listed by the second implementation (four contradictions, about 30 gaps; ledger, status to confirm).
9. **Tax credits**: no child and dependent care credit; EITC reach is low (11.9% against 15.3%) because the model has no part-time work (ledger).
10. **Who is simulated**: working-age adults and their families; the Hub should say so (ledger). The labour-force scope option exists.
11. **Capacity of the community businesses is for the whole population**, not by zone or by sector. One utility share stands for electricity, gas and water.
12. **No private firms, banks or bond market.** The central-bank rule is a reduced form and has no channel to the price of essentials. There is no expectations channel.
13. **Capital income is not in the price rule's income**, and the automation dividend raises no investment.
14. **Displaced adults' outcomes by fifth of starting wealth** are not stored.
15. **Health, security and output per hour**: no opened source sizes health and security raising output per hour (left out of the automation study).

## C. The Hub and its figures
16. **Audit-flagged figures still live on the Hub**, many only in the PDFs: $847B net savings, "65% lower inflation", "15 percentage point" (it is 13), 85%/98% poverty reduction and $82,000 median wealth with a 95% interval, "10,000 iterations", elasticity −0.71 (it is −1.6), a steady state of 11.8% under a "below 5%" theorem, "14% of GDP" (about 11%), the Bristol Pound "£5 billion" and the 2.86 multiplier (it is 1.95). The main corrections package's first 22 items are not landed (ledger).
17. **168 cited external figures not yet opened** (`data/claims.csv`, "cited, not opened"; ledger).
18. **The θ "Monte Carlo calibration"**: no record it was ever run (ledger).
19. **The BLEI page may state the simulation's poverty line inverted** (ledger; status to confirm).
20. **The release data lacks series the BLEI visuals and the Five Measures chart need** (ledger; status to confirm).
21. **The Hub's 32-item site audit**: Gini comparability after the cost-of-living adjustment, terminology, sourcing gaps, AI-authorship disclosure, methodological transparency (ledger; status unknown).

## D. Process before a release
22. Outside readings of the results before they are published: done for the automation study (two readers), not yet for the release's own regenerated figures.
